pr_title: Stop a stuck BlockingCollection.Take operation that caused thread leak on the client.
pr_comments:
Removed Dispose and added 2 extra exception catch blocks.
Looks good. Do you want to squash before I merge? (and potentially address that minor comment?)
Done: fixed logging, squashed, rebased. 
I assume this is going into master (1.2, right?).  If there is a 1.1.3 could I get this fix in there as well?
Alex, I  not sure what is the release plan, but there is also an easy short term fix that you could do on your side: just put a short sleep in between the client init attempts, instead of a tight loop. It will cause much less threads to leak. Also worth mentionint that those threads are just stuck, not really consuming CPU. So it doesn't appear to be  a critical bug.
We are currently using polly with an exponential backoff on re-init.  The threads do appear to be "just stuck" but when the total thread count gets excessive (400+ oooops) the context switch/sec kills the box.
Because we can pull nugets on a private repo I can live with not getting something released in the short term.    I was just hoping to identify what release this will be going into.
@amccool glad that you could work around it. Not high priority I assume, but yes, if there is a 1.1.3 we can definitely include this fix as well.

issue_context.title: Repeated call to Orleans.GrainClient.Initialize cause growing thread count
issue_context.body:
We have a service which starts before the silos have finished starting up.  We are seeing an increasing thread count if there is a delay getting the silos up.

This code produces the same effect.

> ```
>         for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)
>         {
>             try  { Orleans.GrainClient.Initialize();  }
>             catch (Exception ex)
>             {  }
>         }
> ```

The thread count increases on each call to `GrainClient.Initialize`, occasionally the total count will decrement, but overall the thread count continues to climb, and does not drop (even after hours with no more calls to `GrainClient.Initialize`

It appears that a majority of the threads have a stack similar to this, waiting at the `Orleans.RuntimeQueue.Take` on `System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection<Message>.TryTakeWithNoTimeValidation`

> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim.WaitUntilCountOrTimeout+0x90
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim.Wait+0x31a
> System.dll!System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1.TryTakeWithNoTimeValidation+0x15d
> System.dll!System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1.TryTake+0xc1
> System.dll!System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1.Take+0x22
> Orleans.dll!Orleans.Runtime.RuntimeQueue`1.Take+0x1a
> Orleans.dll!Orleans.Messaging.ProxiedMessageCenter.WaitMessage+0x3e
> Orleans.dll!Orleans.OutsideRuntimeClient.RunClientMessagePump+0x55
> Orleans.dll!<>c__DisplayClass3.<StartInternal>b__2+0x2f
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.Tasks.Task.Execute+0x6e
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.ExecutionContext.RunInternal+0x285
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.ExecutionContext.Run+0x9
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.Tasks.Task.ExecuteWithThreadLocal+0x2c5
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.Tasks.Task.ExecuteEntry+0x85
> mscorlib.dll!System.Threading.ThreadPoolWorkQueue.Dispatch+0x1ea
comments:
Can you please try something for me:
try putting Orleans.GrainClient.UnInitialize inside the catch block. 
Does that take the thread count down?
`Orleans.GrainClient.UnInitialize` helps slow velocity, but the total is still growing.
OK, we will take a look. That one is easy to repro.
Found it:
we pass `CancellationToken` to `ProxiedMessageCenter.WaitMessage`, but ignore it and don't pass it to `PendingInboundMessages.Take();`, so the Take is blocked (forever).

**We should NOT pass `CancellationToken` to Blocking Collection Take**. We saw in the past (albeit a very long time ago), that this caused a dramatic throughput decrease. Passing CancellationToken  to Blocking Collection caused a lot of internal spinning inside  Blocking Collection (to check the token), and it drained perf.
Its possible that was solved in later .NET version, but I would still avoid using it.

Instead, I would just hard kill this thread, or Dispose the Blocking Collection  or call CompleteAdding. Something that will unblock the Take, but without the constant spinning on  CancellationToken  cost.

In `AsynchQueueAgent`, which also uses  Blocking Collection in the same way, we use `CompleteAdding`. That is the way to go:

```
    //   T:System.InvalidOperationException:
    //     The underlying collection was modified outside of this System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1
    //     instance, or the System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1 is empty
    //     and the collection has been marked as complete for adding.
    public T Take();
```
Cool. Btw, the alternative wouldn't work. Passing a cancellation token to the StartNew wouldn't abort a Task mid-process. It is only used to avoid starting the task if it was canceled prior to it being executed.
Heh, replied before you edited the comment :p
Yes, I figured that out. 
Fix is in #1351.
trying a CompleteAdding in ProxiedMessageCenter.

> ```
>     public void PrepareToStop()
>     {
>         // put any pre stop logic here.
>         PendingInboundMessages.CompleteAdding();
>     }
> ```

This seems to work.   But of course your fix is much preferred.   I will test https://github.com/dotnet/orleans/pull/1351 right now.
running an extended test with #1351 so far so good!
#1351 is good by me.   I do see this exception going by, but nothing adverse appears to be associated with it.

```
[2016-01-29 08:25:16.992 GMT     4      ERROR   100021  Messaging.ProxiedMessage
Center  172.18.4.211:0] !!!!!!!!!! Unexpected error getting an inbound message

Exc level 0: System.ArgumentNullException: Value cannot be null.
   at System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim.Wait(Int32 millisecondsTimeout, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1.TryTakeWithNoTimeValidation(T& item, Int32 millisecondsTimeout, CancellationToken cancellationToken, CancellationTokenSource combinedTokenSource)
   at System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1.TryTake(T& item, Int32 millisecondsTimeout, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at System.Collections.Concurrent.BlockingCollection`1.Take()
   at Orleans.Runtime.RuntimeQueue`1.Take() in C:\Users\Alex\Source\Repos\orleans\src\Orleans\Runtime\RuntimeQueue.cs:line 112
   at Orleans.Messaging.ProxiedMessageCenter.WaitMessage(Categories type, CancellationToken ct) in C:\Users\Alex\Source\Repos\orleans\src\Orleans\Messaging\ProxiedMessageCenter.cs:line 328
```
Issue should be fixed by #1351.
BTW, @amccool please comment back here if after grabbing the latest fix you still see that unexpected exception... you shouldn't any more.
We are currently testing #1351 via private nugets

review_comments:
Regarding the comment at https://github.com/dotnet/orleans/issues/1350#issuecomment-176641395 :

hmmm, that's very odd, but I guess it has to do with Disposing the blocking collection at the same time that the `Take` is initiating, and getting into a weird state. I was trying to follow the code in the framework, but couldn't find an `ArgumentNullException` being thrown from `SemaphoreSlim.Wait` directly. Probably some function got inlined and it's not showing in the stack trace, and the code is very tough to follow. Any chance we can delay disposing somehow? If not, it might make to catch ArgumentNullException (although I dislike that, but it's better than having a catch-all clause for all exceptions to be treated equally, when we know this exception happens harmlessly)
I think I will just remove the Dispose completely. Its redundant. I should not have put it. CompleteAdding is just enough. No need to "smash kill with a hammer" if a clean stop does the work. 
If we did want Dispose (which I think we do not now), then we need to wait for this thread to finish first and dispose only after we know there are no usages.
Sure, although this actually might have some unmanaged resources, since it's using semaphores. Still it might be fine.
Catching  InvalidOperationException still makes sense though according to docs
